message.content:
**Freezing point of water at 10 kPa**

| Pressure | Approximate freezing (melting) point of water |
|----------|----------------------------------------------|
| 101.3 kPa (1 atm) | 0 °C |
| 10 kPa (≈ 0.1 atm) | **≈ –2.2 °C** |

---

### Why it’s lower than 0 °C

Water’s phase diagram shows that the melting point of ice decreases as the external pressure is lowered. At the triple point (0.01 °C, 0.006 atm ≈ 0.6 kPa) ice, liquid water, and vapor coexist. Below this pressure, ice melts at temperatures below 0 °C. At 10 kPa (about one‑tenth of atmospheric pressure), the equilibrium temperature between ice and liquid water is roughly –2.2 °C.

### Quick estimate

A simple linear approximation using the Clausius–Clapeyron relation gives a slope of about –0.01 °C per kPa for the ice–water boundary near 0 °C. Over a drop of 91 kPa (from 101.3 kPa to 10 kPa), this yields:

\[
\Delta T \approx -0.01^\circ\text{C/kPa} \times 91\,\text{kPa} \approx -0.9^\circ\text{C}
\]

However, the actual dependence is slightly steeper at lower pressures, leading to a freezing point closer to –2 °C rather than –0.9 °C. Empirical data from the water phase diagram confirm the –2.2 °C value.

---

**Bottom line:** At 10 kPa, water freezes at about **–2.2 °C**.
